6abf7f884bc3da1e: HAVANA, Oct 28 — Kevin Martinez has come up with a creative new way to avoid shutting his restaurant when water runs low in Cuba, a common source of frustration for the business owner.
The US energy blockade on the communist-run island has caused problems along the line of supply, so Martinez decided to drill downwards and find his own source.
His business is located in the Matanzas province, 100 kilometres east of Havana and one of the regions particularly affected by the shortages.
The issue affects nearly 29 per cent of Cuba’s 9.4 million inhabitants, according to official figures, with the situation worsening significantly since January due to the US energy blockade.
The subsequent crisis has made prolonged blackouts the norm, which in turn reduces the water supply, as pumping depends primarily on electric turbines.
“On several occasions we had to close the establishment because we didn’t have any water...and that’s what brought us to the point of having to dig the well,” Martinez told AFP.
“I never imagined I’d have to be digging a well, just as I never imagined I’d have to be cooking with coal or installing solar panels,” he said.
The decision to drill, although “a bit expensive,” sets him free from paying for water deliveries three times a week.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Cars drive along a street in Havana October 26, 2026. Water does not reach the homes of 2.7 million Cubans, Yunior Gonzalez, a senior official at the national water company, told AFP. — AFP pic
‘Daily struggle’
Water does not reach the homes of 2.7 million Cubans, Yunior Gonzalez, a senior official at the national water company, told AFP.
“Between 80 and 85 per cent of the water” supplied has to be pumped to get to these households, he said, adding that equipment breakdowns, leaks and drought have exacerbated the problem.
Water difficulties are forcing many Cubans to haul the precious resource for long distances, transporting it via wheelbarrows, bicycles, car trunks and even horse-drawn carts.
Maykel Aguilar, 30, patiently filled a 200-liter tank and several buckets at a pipe connected to a spring on a street in the capital’s old town.
He then must use a wheelbarrow to get it to his home before heaving it up a flight of stairs.
“One little trip like that is enough for a load of laundry, cleaning the house, and cooking, and just like that you’re out of water,” Aguilar said.
Neighbours line up in the same spot, marking their place with tanks, buckets and jerrycans.
“The power outages here happen every day and we have to keep hauling water,” said 40-year-old mother of two Yusimy Guerra.
“It’s a daily struggle,” she sighed.
Water scarcity adds to Cuba’s runaway inflation, while food and medicine also run low amid mounting social unrest.
Municipalities in Havana have recorded several women-led protests over water shortages in recent months.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Residents collect potable water from a public supply point in Havana October 5, 2026. Water scarcity adds to Cuba’s runaway inflation, while food and medicine also run low amid mounting social unrest. — AFP pic
‘Thieves’

More and more Cubans are drilling wells on their properties, building cisterns in their yards, installing tanks and even resorting to so-called “water thieves” — pumps that suck the trickle of water from the mains and force it into their homes.
Several of these installations in the same neighbourhood can reduce the pressure in the network and make it even harder for other households to access water.
Well digger Elizardo Cardoso, who found water 10 meters below the ground at Martinez’s restaurant, says his trade is in high demand.
Water agent Gonzalez meanwhile said the government is moving forward with transforming the sector’s energy mix as a way to reduce dependence on the faulty national power grid.
More than 870 solar-powered water pumps have already been installed out of the 1,300 planned, benefiting half a million Cubans across the country, he said.
The Albear Aqueduct, one of Havana’s main sources of water supply, recently gained two brand-new, gigantic backup generators that run on diesel.
But “they are very expensive programmes,” Gonzalez cautioned. — AFP
14c5b8fc8ba1de0e: MONTREAL, Oct 28 — Young Canadians testified yesterday to a “sense of despair” during a landmark climate trial over the federal government’s alleged climate policy failures and the “scary” consequences of global warming.

The latest testimony from the 15 plaintiffs who brought the suit, all aged 17 to 25, is part of a growing global movement among environmental activists seeking to use courts to force government accountability on climate change.
“I want the court to know that we are doing this for our future,” Sadie Vipond said on the stand.
The 20-year-old student hails from Calgary, in western Canada, where she described thick smoke and overwhelming heat that descends year after year on her hometown.
Wildfires are “something we had to be more and more aware of,” Vipond said, adding that she had to evacuate her home in 2013 because of flooding.
“It again brought this sense of despair” in 2022 when the floods returned.

Members of the legal team and some of the 15 plaintiffs of the first youth climate trial in Canada pose at Federal court in Vancouver on the first day in the La Rose v. His Majesty the King trial October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Sophia Sidarous, a 25-year-old member of First Nation, gave emotional testimony about the threat climate change poses to her community’s traditional activities.
“Someone actually died from the heat during a powwow,” she said, describing a traditional Indigenous gathering where she lives in Nova Scotia, in eastern Canada.
She described the frustration of belonging to a community of hunters while “we have moose and salmon and various other species that are declining.”

Climate science professor Kirsten Zickfeld, of Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, also testified for nearly three hours to explain to the court the “increase in the intensity and frequency of extreme heat events, of droughts, of heavy rainfall events and also of rapid sea level rise.”
“Canada’s carbon budget is essentially zero or negative,” Zickfeld added, noting that such a burden “will be passed on to future generations.”
Supporters of the first federal youth climate trial in Canadian history hold up signs during a rally outside the Vancouver Art Gallery in Vancouver October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Overall, the plaintiffs aim to prove that successive governments have violated their constitutional rights to life and security by failing to protect them from the threats posed by climate change.

Canadian targets currently call for a 40-45 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 2005 levels, but Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has already indicated those benchmarks may be missed.
The lawsuit, first filed in 2019, was initially dismissed. In 2023, a federal appeals court ruled the youths were entitled to a trial. — AFP
04fb6dfd792e2f58: WESLACO (Texas), Oct 28 — Formerly a Democratic stronghold, the predominantly Hispanic region of southern Texas has swung rightward in recent years, helping Republicans to a narrow majority in Congress and highlighting a broader shift in Latino voter sentiment.
Now, with control of Congress up for grabs in the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats are hoping a star singer running for office will woo voters back.

Latin Grammy-winner Bobby Pulido, known as the “Golden Boy” of Tejano music, is vying to flip Texas’s 15th congressional district, which stretches from the outskirts of San Antonio south to the Mexico border.
With a population that is over 80 per cent Latino, the district has been represented since 2023 by Republican Monica De La Cruz.
She, like Pulido, grew up in the border area known as the Rio Grande Valley — but her father was not a Tejano music pioneer.

Now 53, Pulido has mostly turned his focus from music to politics during the campaign, but he took to the stage at a rally Sunday in the city of Weslasco alongside the band Los Tigres del Norte, performing their hit song La Puerta Negra (The Black Door).

De La Cruz has hit Pulido for his lack of experience, arguing the election was not about choosing a singer for a quinceanera coming-of-age party, but whom voters should trust with their family’s future.
Pulido took the dig in stride, offering to perform under the banner “Make Quinceaneras Great Again,” a parody of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People sing along Los Tigres del Norte and Bobby Pulido during a joint campaign event in Weslaco, Texas October 25, 2026.
‘We are good people’

Pulido has tied or taken a slight lead over De La Cruz in polls, as high gas prices caused by Trump’s war with Iran and heavy-handed immigration raids push Latino voters away from supporting Republicans.
“Let’s break a record and send a message that they can’t mess with us anymore. We are good people in the Rio Grande Valley,” Pulido told the crowd of thousands at Sunday’s rally.

In today’s polarised US politics, Pulido has aimed to bring people together across the aisle for support, sporting a campaign slogan that says: “I’m not team Red or team Blue. South Texas, I’m team You.”
“Families stopped talking right now because somebody voted for Trump and somebody didn’t,” he said. “I don’t care what happened in the past. We need to look at the future.”
One of the big focus points of his campaign has been dealing with migration along the US-Mexico border.
“I believe we can secure the border without destroying families and our local economy in the process,” Pulido said in a campaign video.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for US House Bobby Pulido speaks during the Voto Latino’s ‘Ready. Go. Vote.’ campaign rally outside of the Mustang Lounge Night Club in Weslaco, Texas October 25, 2026. — Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP pic
‘He’s from here’
Rally attendee Joe Jimenez, 44, told AFP he had previously voted for De La Cruz but now supports Pulido.

“He’s going to do a good job not because he’s a singer, it’s because he’s from here and he not only represents us but has gone through a lot of things that we have done,” Jimenez said, adding that he felt De La Cruz “let us down.”

A 2016 video of Pulido has generated controversy, in which he pretends to urinate on Trump’s star along the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The candidate has said the gesture was a joke performed with a water bottle.
Margarita Ramirez, a 49-year-old from Pulido’s hometown of Edinburg, said she was supporting the singer.
“He has been very honest in his work as a musician, and so why would he not be honest in his work as a politician? He’s not someone seeking to cause scandals. He’s a family man,” she told AFP. — AFP
ba826d6283a7d219: PARIS, Oct 28 — Climate change must be declared a “global health emergency” to shape governments’ policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said today.

Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world’s population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70 per cent of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.

Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were “three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement” of 2015.
“That’s roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat,” she told a news conference.
And “68 per cent of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change.”
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

An aerial view shows villagers swimming above coral reefs off Nadir Beach, approximately 52 kilometres from Nadi October 5, 2026. Almost all shallow-water coral reefs around the world are at ‘extremely high risk’ of disappearing by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have “an integrated approach so that we’re not responding to emergency after emergency”.
Instead, she called for “a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward”.

To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.

Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world’s land surface for at least one month.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows dead coral lying along a beach at Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India’s Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.

South-east Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 per cent and 3.2 per cent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 per cent for Europe and 1.5 per cent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO’s 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached US$2.1 trillion (RM8.5 trillion) in 2025 — double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 per cent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in “at least” 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.

Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach US$316 million in 2024, 84 per cent of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.

Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers’ work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.

And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation. — AFP

3d1314c4ccbf14f4: Intel has become the latest target for Good Jobs First, which questions why the chipmaker continues to receive tax breaks from key states, long after setting up shop there, and laying off thousands of workers in those regions.

The non-profit organization, which promotes accountability in economic development, says the chipmaker promised billions of dollars in investment and thousands of high-tech jobs for the areas surrounding its manufacturing plants in Hillsboro, Oregon, and Rio Rancho, New Mexico.

Its report, The Bleeding Edge: How the Public Pays the Costs of Intel’s Semiconductor Manufacturing, claims that Intel's property tax breaks cost these communities more than $1.2 billion in lost revenue since 2015, and the brunt of the shortfall has largely fallen on schools funded by those local governments.

For Oregon, Good Jobs First says that property tax abatements from Intel's use of the Strategic Investment Program (SIP) exempted it from at least $1.14 billion, while Hillsboro schools lost $891 million in revenue from 2017 through 2025.
During the same timeframe, Intel paid Oregon $552.4 million in fees, or less than a third of the value of its tax breaks.

In New Mexico, the figures are lower, but still significant. The report puts Chipzilla's property tax exemptions from Industrial Revenue Bonds (IRBs) at $99.6 million in foregone revenue since 2017, while Rio Rancho’s Public Schools lost an estimated $43.4 million over the same nine-year period. Here, the company paid $41.6 million in required payments in lieu of taxes from 2017 through 2025, shared among affected local governments.
Good Jobs First also notes that despite these subsidies, Intel was awarded billions under the CHIPS Act funding from the US federal government.
However, the situation with that is somewhat complex, as the company secured an initial $7.86 billion under the Biden administration, of which $2.2 billion is believed to have been paid out.

The incoming Trump administration, however, decided to rethink the scheme, and ended up making an $8.9 billion deal for 10 percent of Intel’s common stock, made up of the remaining $5.7 billion of the CHIPS Act cash plus an additional $3.2 billion under the Secure Enclave program to make semiconductors for the military.

At the same time, the chipmaker is estimated by Good Jobs First to have laid off more than 4,700 workers at its facilities in Oregon and New Mexico over the past three years, as the company wrestled with restructuring efforts and dramatic losses.
(These are just a fraction of Intel’s total layoffs during the period.)

The issue, according to the non-profit, is that these sites are established Intel facilities which the company has operated for decades. They already have the facilities, infrastructure, skilled workers, and other necessities that a new site might require investment for. Are continued tax breaks truly necessary, Good Jobs First asks, or are they just subsidizing business decisions Intel would make anyway?

It says Intel’s track record in Oregon and New Mexico should be taken as important lessons for other communities considering becoming a home to semiconductor manufacturing, and recommends questioning whether state and local tax breaks are even necessary.

"Tax incentives are supposed to encourage investment, not provide companies with an ongoing stream of public support for decades," said Good Jobs First Research Analyst and report author Kristan Wong Karinen.

"Intel has received tax breaks at these campuses for generations, and local leaders should be asking hard questions about why those subsidies are still necessary, especially with the billions of dollars in federal grants and tax credits they receive from the CHIPS Act."

We asked Intel for a statement regarding these claims by Good Jobs First, and in response it told us: "Intel works closely with governments in the regions where we operate to leverage incentives that support leading-edge semiconductor R&D and manufacturing. We are not providing additional details beyond what's available in our annual reports."

Recent targets for the non-profit have been datacenters, and the states offering tax incentives for developers and operators to build within their jurisdiction. Some states were losing billions in lost revenue to server farm projects, while others were failing to disclose their tax shortfall. ®

928f5ef002139c1e: KUALA LUMPUR: Veteran actor and director M Jamil, 62, has officially divorced his wife, Shahrila Markom, after eight months of court proceedings.
According to Harian Metro, the Gombak Lower Syariah Court in Selayang confirmed the single-talak divorce today.
The legal process began in February when Shahrila filed for divorce.
At a court hearing on Sept 28, Shahrila was represented by lawyer Nabila Abdul Rahim, while Muhammad Luqmanulhakim Ahmad appeared for M Jamil.
Judge Maizatul Aliza Chee Din allowed M Jamil to appoint his 28-year-old son, Sadiq, as a family arbitrator to help mediate the dispute amicably.
Speaking to Harian Metro via text message, M Jamil, who was a popular artiste in the 1980s, said he accepts the outcome: "Alhamdulillah. Everything has been settled amicably. Syukur Alhamdulillah.
"We separated with one talak by the court, and our marriage ends here. It is officially over," he said.

M Jamil and Shahrila married on May 24, 2014, following the death of his third wife, Siti Rohani Wahid, in 2010. Over their 12 years together, they had two daughters: Sarimah Salma, 11, and Laila Jamila, 9.
Tensions reportedly mounted last November when Shahrila left the family home with both children.
M Jamil has reportedly not seen his daughters since then.
Both children are currently in Shahrila's care.
M Jamil, son of 84-year-old veteran actress Datuk Sarimah Ahmad, has been in declining health since suffering a stroke eight years ago.
He also struggles with diabetes complications, which previously required the amputation of the little toe on his left foot.
Across his four marriages, M Jamil has fathered 11 children.
He currently lives with two of his children from his late wife, Siti Rohani.
ff5da78a35b5e7dd: KUALA LUMPUR: Perikatan Nasional (PN) memfailkan permohonan secara ex parte bagi mendapatkan kebenaran memulakan prosiding komital terhadap Ketua Pengarah Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM) Zulfikar Ahmad atas dakwaan menghina mahkamah.
Permohonan itu difailkan Setiausaha Agung PN Takiyuddin Hassan bersama empat individu lain dengan menamakan Zulfikar sebagai responden tunggal.
Peguam yang mewakili gabungan itu, Rafique Rashid Ali, mengesahkan permohonan berkenaan telah difailkan.
PN mendakwa JPPM sengaja bertindak mendahului keputusan mahkamah dengan membatalkan pendaftaran gabungan itu ketika permohonan semakan kehakiman dan penangguhan pelaksanaan masih belum selesai.
PN mendakwa tindakan itu bertujuan mengganggu serta menghalang proses pentadbiran keadilan, selain menyebabkan permohonan semakan kehakimannya tidak lagi membawa sebarang kesan.
Menurut pemohon, tindakan Zulfikar dilakukan dengan pengetahuan bahawa prosiding berkenaan masih berjalan dan perkara yang dipertikaikan masih dalam pertimbangan mahkamah.
Mereka mendakwa tindakan itu mempunyai kesan mengganggu, menghalang dan mendahului proses keadilan dalam kes berkenaan.
Pengurusan kes secara kamar ditetapkan pada 12 Nov.

Pada 5 Okt, PN memfailkan permohonan semakan kehakiman terhadap JPPM dengan memohon, antaranya perintah certiorari untuk membatalkan notis bertarikh 23 Sept yang menggantung aktiviti gabungan itu bagi tempoh tidak ditentukan.

PN turut mencabar notis tunjuk sebab bertarikh 22 Sept yang mengarahkannya menjelaskan mengapa pendaftarannya tidak sepatutnya dibatalkan, selain memohon mahkamah mengisytiharkan kedua-dua notis itu tidak sah dan terbatal.
Pada 13 Okt, Mahkamah Tinggi memberi kebenaran kepada PN untuk memulakan prosiding semakan kehakiman.
Seminggu kemudian, RoS membatalkan pendaftaran gabungan itu.

Pada 22 Okt, Mahkamah Tinggi membenarkan penangguhan pelaksanaan pembatalan pendaftaran tersebut, sekali gus membolehkan PN bertanding dalam PRN Melaka akan datang menggunakan lambang gabungan itu sendiri.

8fb68ef688ba964f: KUALA LUMPUR: Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) merancang untuk memperkenalkan konsep 'cottage hospital' dengan menaik taraf klinik kesihatan terpilih di kawasan pedalaman bagi memperluas akses perkhidmatan kesihatan kepada penduduk setempat.
Menteri Kesihatan Dzulkefly Ahmad berkata inisiatif itu melibatkan penambahbaikan kemudahan tertentu bagi klinik kesihatan di kawasan yang mempunyai akses terhad kepada hospital.

Antara fasiliti yang dikenal pasti setakat ini ialah Klinik Kesihatan Tekek di Pulau Tioman, Pahang; Klinik Kesihatan Telupid dan Klinik Kesihatan Nabawan di Sabah serta Klinik Kesihatan Sungai Asap di Sarawak.

"Inisiatif ini bertujuan memperluas akses kepada rawatan pesakit dalam yang bersesuaian, mendekatkan perkhidmatan kesihatan kepada penduduk setempat, terutamanya di pedalaman, dan mengurangkan perjalanan yang jauh untuk mendapatkan rawatan di hospital, sekali gus mengurangkan kesesakan di hospital.

"Inisiatif ini mencerminkan komitmen KKM untuk membangunkan sistem penyampaian perkhidmatan kesihatan yang lebih bersepadu, responsif terhadap keperluan setempat dan mapan selain memastikan akses yang saksama tanpa mengira lokasi geografi," katanya.
Beliau berkata demikian ketika menggulung perbahasan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan 2027 (Belanjawan 2027) bagi KKM di Dewan Rakyat.

Dzulkefly berkata konsep berkenaan turut diamalkan beberapa negara termasuk United Kingdom yang menaik taraf klinik kesihatan terpilih di kawasan luar bandar dengan pelbagai kemudahan, termasuk wad pemerhatian.

Beliau berkata usaha lain ialah penstrukturan semula fungsi dan peranan fasiliti kesihatan primer, termasuk klinik desa, klinik komuniti dan klinik di Pusat Transformasi Bandar (UTC), serta menilai keperluan menaik taraf, menggabungkan atau membangunkan fasiliti baharu berdasarkan kepadatan penduduk serta keperluan kesihatan setempat.

Sementara itu, KKM akan memperluas pelaksanaan Program Penyumberluaran Perkhidmatan Hospital (HSOP) daripada 14 kepada 16 bidang perkhidmatan pada 2027, susulan peningkatan peruntukan daripada RM144 juta tahun ini kepada RM200 juta tahun depan.
Beliau berkata dua bidang baharu yang akan diperkenalkan ialah ujian kultur Mycobacterium tuberculosis bagi penyakit tibi dan ujian genetik pranatal.

Dzulkefly berkata pelaksanaan HSOP yang memanfaatkan kapasiti sektor swasta berjaya mengurangkan tempoh menunggu pesakit secara purata antara dua hingga 10 minggu, selain membantu menangani kesesakan di hospital kerajaan.

"Sebagai contoh, tempoh menunggu bagi pembedahan pintasan jantung (CABG) berjaya dikurangkan sebanyak 18 minggu, daripada 50 kepada 32 minggu manakala rawatan radioterapi bagi kanser prostat berkurangan daripada 21 kepada lapan minggu.
"Tempoh menunggu bagi pemeriksaan tomografi berkomputer (CT) jantung pula berkurangan sebanyak 11 minggu daripada 24 kepada 13 minggu," katanya.

Dzulkefly berkata jumlah pesakit yang menerima manfaat daripada HSOP turut meningkat 22.2% kepada 51,159 pesakit menerusi 14 bidang perkhidmatan berbanding 41,858 pesakit bagi 10 bidang perkhidmatan sebelum ini.
Dalam perkembangan lain, beliau berkata KKM masih menunggu hasil siasatan penuh pihak berkuasa berhubung isu Perkhidmatan Doktor Udara sebelum perkara berkenaan dibentangkan kepada Jemaah Menteri.
Penjelasan lanjut akan diberikan di Dewan Rakyat selepas proses itu selesai bagi memastikan maklumat yang disampaikan adalah telus, tuntas dan menyeluruh.
3eacfea6f34edf7c: John Healey is announcing his financial update – here are the main points, with political analysis Budget 2026 live – latest updates John Healey starts by saying that his budget is “delivered at a time when global uncertainties and pressures are swirling worldwide and hitting people here at home”. Healey says he will meet the fiscal rule that day-to-day spending must be covered by tax receipts, and the investment rule that government debt, defined as public sector net financial liabilities, must be falling as a percentage of GDP in the third year of the forecast. The government will have £15bn of headroom in 2029-30 and £20bn in 2030-31, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility, the government’s forecaster. Government borrowing will be 4.2% of GDP this year, 3.4% next year, then 2.9%, 2.1% and 1.8% by 2030-31, the OBR says. Predictions of slowing growth were wrong, Healey says. The OBR says GDP will grow by 1.2% this year, 1% next year, 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029, 1.7% in 2030 and 1.6% in 2031. In March the OBR had predicted GDP growth of 1.1% in 2026, rising to 1.6% in 2027 and 2028, and dropping to 1.5% in 2029 and 2030. Government debt is forecast to be 83.2% of GDP this year, 83.8% next year then falling to 83.1%, 82.3% and 81.7% in the following years. Labour’s priority is cheaper energy, Healey says. He announces a series of measures to try to cut bills, including scrapping a levy on bills to fund hydrogen to lower bills and moving older renewables onto fixed-price contracts. Healey says the government will extend a VAT cut through the winter and spring to July, taking £50 pounds off the annual price cap. He confirms the government is abolishing standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes in a move it says will save two-thirds of households an average of £45 a year. He says 20m households in council tax bands A to D will receive a £100 energy payment paid directly into bank accounts. It will cost £2.6bn, he says. Fuel duty will be frozen for the 16th year in a row. Every government forecast over that time has pretended it will then rise in future years to raise more cash, only for the freeze to continue. Healey increases the higher mileage rate for people who use their cars for work from £0.25 to £0.30 a mile. Healey says he will remove import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, to reduce their shop prices as trailed before the budget. On paternity leave, self-employed fathers will be eligible for paternity leave pay for the first time. Healey says he will increase the threshold for small business rate relief from £12,000 to £18,000, giving a tax break to 70,000 smaller firms. On gambling, machine game duty will rise from 20% to 25% for higher stakes machines. Adult gaming centres and vape shops will not qualify for business rates relief. Online marketplace sellers will be targeted to ensure they are unable get around VAT. Healey says there will be new funding from HMRC to improve compliance and stronger powers to collect overdue tax from those who “can clearly afford to pay but ignore repeated contact”. There will be no change on tax on income from dividends, and no change on tax to income from employment. Healey confirms he will reverse his predecessor’s decision to cut the tax-free allowance on cash individual savings accounts (ISAs) from £20,000 to £12,000 a year from April. Healey says he celebrates the role that banks play in the UK economy, but they will pay an extra 3% on the bank surcharge for 15 months from January. In a budget characterised by relative secrecy, raising taxes on banks was one of the policies that did leak out beforehand. PW: No big surprises here, with the bulk of the changes being technical or incremental. The one exception is the expected increase in the windfall tax on bank profits, which will be set aside to pay for measures to help with energy bills. With this comes a direct challenge from Healey to Kemi Badenoch, who speaks next: does she back this or not? Continue reading...
2b840ceba113fe73: KUALA LUMPUR: Property developer Oriental Interest Bhd will not proceed with the proposed RM280 million acquisition of the entire equity interest in Chin Hin (Jitra) Sdn Bhd and CHJ Motor Holdings Sdn Bhd.

In a Bursa Malaysia filing today, Oriental Interest said the company and the vendor, LLSB 1980 Holdings Sdn Bhd, had mutually agreed to terminate, revoke and rescind the conditional share sale and purchase agreement through a termination agreement dated Oct 28, 2026.

It added that the decision followed a reassessment of the company's business strategies, diversification considerations and the strategic alignment of the proposed acquisitions with its overall business objectives.

"Among other factors, the company took into consideration the longer than anticipated timeframe and additional resources required to fulfil the relevant regulatory, approval and procedural requirements for completion," said Oriental Interest.
Following the termination, the company said neither party would have any claims against the other arising from the agreement.

"Oriental Interest, through its subsidiaries, remains focused on growing its core property development and general construction businesses, supported by a healthy pipeline of ongoing developments, growing unbilled sales and a sizeable landbank," it added.

To date, Oriental Interest's landbank stood at approximately 814.63 hectares of strategically located development land, providing a strong foundation for future projects and long-term earnings visibility.
ef4e44cc5d6756d0: KUALA LUMPUR: The authorities should exercise restraint before making any decision on Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain's tenure as Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) director-general.

Shuhaily's lawyer, Datuk Baljit Singh Sidhu, said the charge against his client under Section 323 of the Penal Code should be considered in its proper legal context, stressing that the principle of innocent until proven guilty must remain paramount.
He said the offence was non-seizable, ordinarily dealt with as a summons case, as well as being bailable.
He added that it was not a registrable offence under the Registration of Criminals and Undesirable Persons Act 1969.
"Any decision affecting his tenure should be made objectively, with due consideration of the law, the facts and the circumstances of the case," he said.
Baljit also said public sentiment had been overwhelmingly supportive of the work Shuhaily had undertaken so far.
"Under the circumstances, I would urge that we exercise sound judgment, restraint and circumspection before taking any position or making any representation to His Majesty the King.
"The matter deserves careful and responsible consideration," he said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a senior lawyer familiar with the case said any disciplinary action should be proportionate to the alleged offence and supported by clear reasons.
The lawyer, who declined to be named, said the charge was a minor, non-seizable, bailable and compoundable offence under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).
He said suspending or interdicting Shuhaily under the Public Officers (Conduct and Discipline) Regulations 1993 before the court process concluded could be disproportionate.
"Section 260 of the CPC expressly allows offences of this nature to be settled through a compound, which operates in law as an acquittal.

"Any aggressive disciplinary action at this stage circumvents this statutory framework and penalises an officer on the presumption of guilt for a matter the law permits to be resolved externally," he said.
He warned that an unreasonable suspension could be challenged through a judicial review in the High Court, potentially exposing the authorities to legal costs and claims for aggravated damages.

"The legally sound course of action is for the authorities to exercise administrative restraint and allow the judicial process to take its course to avoid hasty action that could trigger costly and embarrassing litigation against the state," he said.
Shuhaily, 54, pleaded not guilty to two charges of voluntarily causing hurt to two Special Branch policemen last month.

Shuhaily, charged as a summoned person, was accused of causing hurt to Lance Corporals Muhammad Ekmal Sofwan Driman, 25, and Mohamad Faiz Saman, 40, at Counter J on the fifth floor of KLIA Terminal 1 between 1.27pm and 1.35pm on Sept 28.
The charges carries a maximum jail term of a year, a fine of up to RM2,000, or both, upon conviction.
Shuhaily was released after a family friend posted bail of RM1,500 with one surety for each charge.
He will return to the court on Nov 25 for case management.
Earlier, Inspector-General of Police Tan Sri Mohd Khalid Ismail said Shuhaily's service status has been referred to the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) for legal advice.
He said Shuhaily's assignment at MCBA was based on a two-year secondment contract from the police, which had received the King's consent.
He said suspension from duty will depend on the A-GC's advice and contract termination must be submitted to the King.

790c2212a82ec7cf: KUALA LUMPUR: Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB) has acquired a logistics property in Bayan Lepas Waterfront, Penang, from Titijaya Land Bhd for RM300 million as part of its strategy to expand its logistics portfolio and strengthen recurring income streams.

b5e79c3f135e3bc3: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — The Court of Appeal today sentenced a headmaster to 20 years in jail and 11 strokes of the cane for making pornography and committing physical sexual assault against a standard six student five years ago.

A three-judge panel, chaired by Justice Datuk Noorin Badaruddin alongside Justices Datuk Mohd Radzi Abdul Hamid and Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid, dismissed Anuar Kintan’s appeal against his conviction and sentence of nine years and eight strokes of the cane imposed by the High Court for the charge of making pornography.

The panel, however, allowed the prosecution’s appeal to overturn the lower court’s decisions to acquit and discharge Anuar on the second charge of physical sexual assault against the victim, who was 12 years old at the time.
The court subsequently convicted him of the charge, sentencing him to 11 years with three strokes of the cane.

Justice Noorin, who delivered the unanimous decision, ordered the sentences to be served consecutively. She also issued a warrant of committal for Anuar, 59, to begin his sentence today. He had previously obtained a stay of execution of the sentence and was released on bail of RM14,000 with one surety pending disposal of his appeal.

The court, meanwhile, upheld the lower court’s decision to acquit and discharge Anuar on the third and fourth charges, which involved physical sexual assault on the girl and uttering words intended to be heard by the victim for sexual purposes.

Justice Noorin said the victim had given direct testimony identifying the accused as the person who took the photographs, and that her testimony had been considered by the Sessions Court judge who accepted it.
She said the existence of the photographs was not an isolated circumstance, but was supported by forensic examination that identified the images in Anuar’s Realme mobile phone.
On the second charge, Justice Noorin said the court disagreed that the alibi evidence presented by Anuar had raised reasonable doubt.
The defence had put forward an alibi in which Anuar’s wife testified that he was at home with her, and not at the school, when the incident occurred.

Justice Noorin said the testimony of the victim’s friend provided material support for the prosecution’s case regarding the accused’s presence at the school on April 3, 2021, and his movements with the victim. Therefore, the alibi evidence presented by the accused did not raise reasonable doubt.

On April 19, 2024, the Sessions Court found Anuar guilty of the first offence for making pornography by taking photos of the victim and sentenced him to three years in jail and two strokes of the cane.

The Sessions Court also sentenced him to an additional one year’s imprisonment and two strokes of the cane under Section 16 (1) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017. The section provides for punishment if an offender commits a sexual crime while holding a position of trust over a child. The sentences were to run consecutively.
The Sessions Court, however, acquitted him of the second, third and fourth charges.
The High Court on Aug 15 last year increased the prison sentence for the first charge to nine years’ imprisonment and eight strokes of the cane and upheld his acquittal for the other three charges.
The offences were committed at a school in Perak in the middle of March 2021 and on April 3, 2021.
At the proceedings today, Anuar was represented by lawyer Amir Khusyairi Mohamad Tanusi while Deputy Public Prosecutors Azlina Mahmod and P. Sarulatha appeared for the prosecution. — Bernama
8935f192bb956677: KUALA LUMPUR: "Do not wait until they are gone to seek them out, for that leads to a regret that never ends."
This is exactly how influencer and singer Cik B, 21, feels today.
Speaking after the recent death of her father, Mohammad Amin Yasin, on Oct 23, she urged people to stay close to their parents while they are still around.
In a video shared by her mother, businesswoman Datuk Seri Vida, Cik B expressed deep regret about her relationship with her late father.
Cik B—whose real name is Nur Edlynn Zamileen Mohammad Amin—said that keeping in touch with your parents is important, whether your family lives together or apart.
"Whether it is your father or mother who is not by your side, try to call or reach out to them. Do not wait until they are gone to try and find them.
"That is my regret. If they are still with us—even if the relationship is strained or distant—try to talk things through and resolve matters amicably," she said.
According to Cik B, children can never truly know what is in a parent's heart, and parents may have changed for the better over time.
Reflecting on her own experience, Cik B shared her deep heartbreak, explaining that she only got to see her father after he had passed away.
"I personally regret that I only saw him once he was gone. We hadn't met face-to-face for a long time; the last time I saw him was when I was very young.
"Regardless, he was still my father, and this regret is endless," she said.
Because of this, she encouraged everyone not to miss the chance to love and stay connected with their parents while they are still here.
"For those who still have parents—even if they are divorced—they remain your parents.
"Reach out to them by phone, even if you cannot meet in person often. At the very least, try to see them two or three times a year," she said.
Cik B, her mother, and her brother were in Jakarta, Indonesia, when they received the sad news.
The family flew back and visited Mohammad Amin's grave in Kelantan yesterday.
Vida—whose real name is Hasmiza Othman—married Mohammad Amin in 2000, and the couple divorced in 2008.
They had four children together: Muhammad Eddie Zuhdie, Muhammad Edrie Zikrie, Cik B, and Muhammad Eric Zaquan.
Tragically, her two older brothers, Muhammad Eddie Zuhdie and Muhammad Edrie Zikrie, passed away in a house fire at their home in Ipoh in 2013, just three days before Hari Raya Aidilfitri.

e8c6c1e72f34fb01: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has stressed that Budget 2027 was formulated to continue promoting Islam, including through specific measures to strengthen pondok religious schools nationwide.

Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said the government had sought the views of Islamic scholars and religious teachers in drawing up the budget to ensure that the development needs of Islam received due attention.
He therefore criticised certain quarters for labelling the leader behind the Madani Government’s Budget 2027 as a “hypocrite”.

“When formulating Budget 2027, we asked what more could be done for Islam and what else could be added. In the past, we neglected pondok institutions and pesantren (Islamic boarding schools), but now we are rebuilding them.

“In the past, we sidelined the syeikhs, religious teachers and tuan-tuan guru (respected religious scholars), but now we invite them and seek their views,” he said when speaking at the Majlis Ilmu MADANI programme at Kompleks Seri Perdana here today, which featured renowned Indonesian preacher Ustaz Dr Abdul Somad Batubara as a guest.

Also present were the Prime Minister’s wife, Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail; Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan; and Weststar Group founder and managing director Tan Sri Dr Syed Azman Syed Ibrahim.
Anwar admitted that he was somewhat angered by the matter but said he remained patient, describing it as a systemic problem.

“When the matter was debated in Parliament, he called the leader a hypocrite and the budget hypocritical. If I were to ask Ustaz Abdul Somad, he would say, ‘Be patient, Pak.’ My heart was boiling, but I remained patient and did not respond.

“I just want to say that this is merely symptomatic of the real problem … those who profess Islam do not help or set a good example in terms of morals, personal conduct, moderation and tolerance,” he said.
Previously, Dewan Rakyat Speaker Tan Sri Johari Abdul had directed Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu) to withdraw the word “hypocrite” that he had used during the debate.

The Prime Minister also expressed his appreciation to Abdul Somad for sharing his knowledge at the programme, adding that the preacher’s advice was always taken seriously in efforts to make Malaysia a better country.
“Ustaz Abdul Somad is now a prominent figure, but he is also controversial in some respects because he is bold in his criticism, which can sometimes be sharp.

“His criticism reaches all those in power, including in Malaysia. However, based on our experience in matters of governance and procedures, we welcome such criticism and try to make improvements,” he said.
ae54869ed07b61f8: GUAYAQUIL: The plane that Argentine authorities say is carrying defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro made a brief stop in Ecuador on Wednesday before flying on to an unknown destination, AFP journalists saw.

Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's runoff election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, boarded a flight to Ecuador after arriving in Argentina on Tuesday night, the latter country's National Directorate of Migration said on X.
The 45-year-old entered Argentina "with valid travel documents and no legal impediment," it added, despite a court order banning his exit.
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters then boarded "a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly SA bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador," the government agency said.
According to data from the Flightradar24 website, the plane took off just after midnight on Wednesday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country's northeast.
That plane landed in Guayaquil shortly before 4am before taking off again less than an hour later, AFP journalists and Flightradar24 data confirmed.
Bolsonaro's final destination is unknown, but the FlightAware website said the plane was headed to Miami.
Baires Fly did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.
The US state department said it would issue visas to the senator and his family.
US media earlier reported, citing anonymous sources, that Bolsonaro had arrived in the US on Tuesday.
Brazil's Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports.
He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.

A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.
'Shameful'
Reports of Bolsonaro's exit from Brazil came as a shock to his political camp.
"We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho told reporters in Brasilia on Tuesday.
"I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," he said.
"That was the only communication we had," he added.
Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Instagram a day earlier that he "never had any intention of leaving the country" and the ban on his exit was a scare tactic.
Lula, who won the election with 51.8% of the vote, called fleeing the country a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration.
Following his loss, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.
Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.
US president Donald Trump, a close ally of Flavio's father and Brazil's former leader Jair Bolsonaro, said that the elections were "rigged".
Bolsonaro seemed like the more likely winner after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.
He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.

ba7f5ac2b22a607f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — The High Court here today dismissed the appeal by former Axis Incorporation Bhd board adviser Lee Koon Huat against his conviction and sentence on four charges of abetting the furnishing of false financial statements to Bursa Malaysia.

In a statement today, the Securities Commission (SC) said Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin held that the prosecution had proven the charges against Lee beyond reasonable doubt at trial and there were no grounds to interfere with the Sessions Court’s decision.
“The High Court further agreed with the SC’s submission that the sentence imposed against Lee was appropriate in view of Lee’s role in the commission of the offences.

“As such, the court dismissed Lee’s appeal against sentence and upheld the sentence imposed by the Sessions Court, being six months’ imprisonment and a fine of RM200,000 for each charge or in default, six months’ imprisonment,” it said.
The statement said, the court allowed Lee’s application for stay of execution in respect of the sentence of imprisonment, but declined to grant a stay in respect of the fine.
“Lee will have to pay a total fine of RM800,000 by today, failing which he will be imprisoned in default of the payment,” said the statement.

The SC said Lee was initially charged at the Sessions Court on 23 March 2013 with four charges under Section 122C(c) read together with Section 122B(a)(bb) of the Securities Industry Act 1983 (SIA) for abetting Axis in the furnishing of false financial statements relating to the revenue of Axis for the financial year 2007.
“Evidence adduced during the trial established that Lee had instructed the inflation of Axis’ reported revenue in its four unaudited quarterly results for the financial year 2007,” it said.

The SC had also previously charged three former Axis executive directors, Lee Han Boon, Saipuddin Lim Abdullah and Koh Tee Jin, with offences relating to the furnishing of false financial statements for the 2007 and 2008 financial years.
All three pleaded guilty and were sentenced to imprisonment terms ranging from one day to 12 months, while Lee Han Boon and Koh were also sentenced to fine of RM200,000 respectively.

Deputy Public Prosecutor Shoba Venu Gobal and prosecuting officers Low Wen Zhen, Eunice Ong, and Amina Qistina Mohd Idris appeared for the SC while Lee was represented by counsel Jason Ng Kau and Caroline Lee. — Bernama
ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania, or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack. 1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest. Caitlyn Collins receives funding from Pivotal, Arnold Ventures, and the Weidenbaum Center on the Economy, Government, and Public Policy at Washington University in St. Louis. She is affiliated with the American Sociological Association, Work and Family Researchers Network, and Council on Contemporary Families. Chloe Gibbs currently receives research funding from Arnold Ventures and Pivotal. She previously served with the President's Council of Economic Advisers from 2022-23 with fellowship support from the Federation of American Scientists.
04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. In 2011-2012 he was the Senior Health Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and from 2023-2025 he was Deputy Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Helen Levy was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. She served as a Senior Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers in 2010-2011.
d24ff8d51ac9d0c5: KUALA LUMPUR: "If my own child wanted to enter the music industry, I wouldn't encourage it at all. The future is truly uncertain," said Persatuan Karyawan Malaysia (Karyawan) president Datuk Freddie Fernandez.
Fernandez shared these thoughts recently on the YouTube channel Lebih Masa, during a segment titled Bukan Sekadar Bicara.

Speaking on the topic "Song Royalties: Who Is Actually Getting Rich?" — moderated by Kamarul Bahrin Haron alongside co-host Datuk Saniboey Mohd Ismail — Fernandez addressed a long-standing issue that continues to trouble the local entertainment industry: royalties.
During the hour-long discussion, Fernandez noted that royalty collection remains unresolved, even though he has spent over 30 years in the industry fighting for the cause.
The session covered the transparency of collection bodies, as well as the royalties earned by the late Tan Sri P. Ramlee and the late Datuk Sudirman Arshad.
He also recalled his early days as a student at St. John's Institution, where he started playing music before forming his band, The Revolvers.
Reflecting on his career, Fernandez admitted to making a costly mistake early on by signing a contract without reading it properly.
"One mistake I made was signing a publishing contract without reading it. At the time, I hadn't been properly informed; I had already approached Warner to handle the distribution of the album.
"We didn't have a record label, so we produced the album using our own funds—covering studio fees and all other production costs—and once it was finished, I simply approached Warner for distribution.
"But within that 'distribution' contract, I suddenly discovered there was a separate 'publishing' agreement under which Warner is entitled to 50 percent of the royalties I receive.
"So, for the past 30 years, I haven't heard a word from Warner—yet every single year, they have been taking half, or 50 percent, of my royalties.
"And this is something that happens to many composers and artistes," he said.
Under the terms of that contract, Fernandez and the lyricist each receive a 25 per cent share, while the remaining 50 per cent goes to Warner.
9d9cf7ac2a1f28b1: Amazon had plenty of new gadgets to share at its Echo hardware event this year, along with updates to the AI-powered Alexa Plus after it became available to everyone in the US in February. But the big news this year is screens: devices with big, beautiful ones, and those that lack them entirely.

There’s the Alexa Photo Frame, which Amazon devices chief Panos Panay describes as “the world’s smartest photo frame” and that doubles as a full Alexa speaker.
