<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that invaded our brains, thought fast, swapped coffins, and hit the art gallery.

First, an ancient viral pandemic that afflicted many of our primate relatives—but somehow missed humans—may help explain how we got so smart (relatively speaking). Then: mammal brains eat crow, an upcycled sarcophagus, and a trip to the starry Provençal summer of 1889.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Your brain on viral content
Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances.

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study.

Retroviruses are infectious agents that can invade the genomes of their hosts and insert copies of their own genetic material, producing long-term evolutionary effects. Researchers have now discovered a family of these endogenous retroviruses called PTERV1—which are abundant in chimpanzees, but absent in humans—that influence brain development.

“Among primates, the human brain stands out as the largest and most complex due in part to an increase in cortical neurons and increase in synaptic connectivity,” said a team led by researchers from Lund University. “With a size roughly three times that of our closest living evolutionary relative, the chimpanzee, it has unique cognitive capabilities.”

“The underlying genetic divergences responsible for these differences are still poorly understood,” the researchers continued, noting that their new findings “reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.”

The team discovered the mechanism using human and chimpanzee brain organoids, which are miniature clusters of neurons grown from stem cells that can model some aspects of brain development. The results revealed chimpanzee-specific PTERV1 insertions on chromosome 19 that silences a gene called LINC00662. In contrast, this gene is active during human brain development, and affects neuronal maturation, development, and outgrowth.

“These PTERV1 insertions are thought to have originated from infections that occurred in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago,” said the team. “PTERV1 elements are found in chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas…Notably, the absence of PTERV1 insertions from the human genome suggests that either the human and chimpanzee lineages did not occupy the same habitat at the time or that germline-competent cells of the human ancestor were resistant to this infection.”

“In summary, this study describes how retroviral insertions contributed to the functional divergence of the human and chimpanzee brain, providing a mechanism by which retroviral infections influenced primate brain speciation,” they added.

In other words, early humans appear to have dodged consequential pandemics that widely infected our primate brethren simply because they had a random immunity to it, or roamed different ranges. While retroviruses are far from the only factor in our cognitive development, it’s still eerie to think that our human brain—that brilliant lump you are using to read these words—is shaped by dumb luck.
In other news…
Another brain to crow about
Schmidbauer, Philipp and Nieder, Andreas. “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain.” Science.

Speaking of interspecies brain-offs, it seems the birds have got us beat—at least when it comes to snap decisions. Scientists have discovered that carrion crows (Corvus corone) can make ultrafast choices in “approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy,” according to a new study.

A pair of researchers observed two crows performing a common discrimination task in which dots on a screen move left, right, up, or down. The crows selected the predominant direction by pecking a target circle on a touchscreen, after which they were rewarded with promptly dispensed treats. The crows performed the task dozens of times at extremely high speeds, achieving an overall choice accuracy of 75 percent (crow 1) and 73 percent (crow 2).

“Having diverged from mammals more than 360 million years ago, birds evolved a distinct nuclear pallium”—a part of the vertebrate forebrain—”that lacks the layered neocortex yet retains key organizational and computational principles characteristic of mammalian brains,” said study authors Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder of the University of Tübingen.
“These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decisionmaking circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control,” the team added.
So if anyone ever calls you a birdbrain, the correct response is “thanks.”
Who is this sarcopha-guy?
Rodwell, Warwick. “Westminster Abbey’s Roman Sarcophagus and its Afterlife.” Journal of the British Archaeological Association.

Archaeologists may have finally discovered the mysterious identity of an ancient skeleton buried in a Roman-era sarcophagus that was first unearthed on the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 200 years ago.

Despite an inscription on the sarcophagus identifying the occupant as Valerius Amandinus—a wealthy Londoner who lived between 300 to 400 AD—the bones likely belong to a medieval monk named Ælfwig, born centuries later in the year 993.

“The burial was of a male, probably in his late forties, and was radiocarbon dated to around the turn of the 11th century,” said study author Rodwell Warwick of Westminster Abbey. “The corpse had been laid in a timber coffin and covered with lime; it was then placed inside the sarcophagus. It is argued that this was the prestigious burial of Abbot Ælfwig.”

The sarcophagus was exhumed and moved to a northern courtyard during King Henry III’s reconstruction of the abbey in the mid-1200s, where it laid for about six centuries. On Easter Monday 1820, the coffin was “wantonly broke by workmen” according to a note from an unknown contemporary archivist. Any grave goods were likely plundered by this crew and the sarcophagus was hastily put back together and reburied with the bones all jumbled up inside. It was then re-discovered in 1869 with a note that the burial “‘had been subjected to violence by a previous examination.”

It turns out anything is recyclable—even sarcophagi. The discovery that this Roman coffin at some point took on another tenant now raises the new question of how the earthly remains of Valerius Amandinus got evicted and where they ultimately wound up.
“The Starry Night”—of July 22, 1889?
Kim, Elijah Jeong-hyun et al. “The actual sky of Van Gogh’s Starry Night: a multidisciplinary reconstruction.” Scientific Reports.

With its vibrant colors and psychedelic swirls, Vincent Van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” is one of the most beloved and recognizable paintings in art history. For years, experts and admirers have debated whether the mesmerizing skyscape, which van Gogh painted during an asylum stay in Provence, was a fantastical portrayal or if the artist included realistic renderings of astronomical phenomena.

Now, a team has proposed that the celestial elements of the painting match with a specific night—July 22, 1889—when “the waning-crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades cluster gather within that narrow frame,” according to a new study. This date conflicts with the conventional timeline of van Gogh painting “The Starry Night” weeks earlier in June.

“The question dividing fantasy from observation remained a matter of qualitative interpretation and was never treated in a physically decidable form,” said researchers led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University. “The approach of this study shifts the burden of proof: if the celestial arrangement on the canvas matches a specific dawn sky, that match itself becomes what the imaginative reading must explain.”

The team’s findings “suggest that the night sky in ‘The Starry Night’ originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating,” they continued. “This framework can extend to historical night paintings as a reproducible scientific art history.”

I love a hyper-niche new subfield—let’s call this one “forensic astroartistry.” Regardless of the painting’s exact date of origin, it has inspired wonder and fascination for more than a century—including these new stellaria of long-lost summer nights.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

035bd7a76af7ff36: From Moaz Nair
On April 21, 2018, the threat of foreign espionage on Malaysian soil turned fatal.

Fadi Mohammad al-Batsh, a Palestinian lecturer and drone specialist, was gunned down in Setapak by two assassins who had tracked his movements. The hit bore all the hallmarks of Israel’s intelligence agency, Mossad.
For Malaysia's National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa), this assassination remains a chilling reminder of why the nation must stay vigilant against foreign intelligence operations.
Yet, until very recently, a massive vulnerability remained completely unaddressed, sitting quietly in the pockets of our nation's leaders – Waze.
The chief secretary to the government’s immediate directive banning civil servants from using Waze represents a massive, long-overdue milestone in digital sovereignty.

While ordinary citizens use navigation apps without a second thought, the technology poses a distinct national security risk for individuals holding strategic government, military or intelligence positions.
For Malaysia’s strategic leaders, deleting Waze is no longer a matter of personal convenience – it is a non-negotiable imperative of national defence.
Who controls the data?
To understand the risk, one must look at who controls the telemetry data.
Although Google purchased Waze in 2013, the legal entity operating the app remains Waze Mobile Ltd, which is registered and incorporated in Israel.

Waze’s terms of service explicitly state that the platform is governed solely by the laws of the state of Israel. Under Israeli national security laws, authorities can legally compel Israeli-registered entities to hand over data trails in the interest of state security.
Furthermore, Waze’s history is deeply intertwined with Israel's military apparatus. Co-founder Uri Levine is a veteran of Unit 8200, Israel's elite military cyber-intelligence unit.

With Israel's commercial tech sector heavily staffed by cyber-warfare veterans, European nations like Germany, Switzerland and France, alongside key Middle Eastern states, refuse to gamble their digital sovereignty on such a high-risk data pipeline.
Malaysia is right to follow their blueprint for protective governance.

By design, Waze continuously logs highly invasive information, including real-time GPS locations, exact travel history and background location data even when the app is closed. Advanced artificial intelligence can easily process this granular data to build highly specific movement profiles.
For a high-ranking Malaysian official, using Waze means outsourcing their daily routine, secure meeting locations and personal vulnerabilities to an entity governed by a foreign power.
The ClearPhish leak
If geopolitical risks feel abstract, the immediate cyber threats are undeniably concrete.

Cyber technology firm ClearPhish recently revealed that a database containing the records of over 7.6 million Waze users is being advertised for sale on a dark web marketplace by cybercriminals. The leaked information includes usernames, unique IDs, real-time GPS coordinates, and full travel histories.
This massive leak proves that user data is never entirely secure. In the hands of bad actors, this data can be used to map routines, launch targeted cyberattacks, or facilitate physical stalking.
When millions of users are exposed globally, relying on foreign proprietary platforms for state transit becomes a gamble Malaysia cannot afford.
Navigating the local alternatives

Securing our national transit does not mean driving blind. The government has aggressively pushed for the adoption of TuJu, a locally developed navigation application created by the Malaysian Highway Authority (LLM) and Prosignal Consortium.
Because TuJu keeps traffic data domestic, it eliminates the threat of foreign legal intervention.
Admittedly, the sudden surge of users following the ban caused TuJu's infrastructure to experience technical disruptions, prompting a public apology and optimisation promises from LLM.
While the app undergoes growing pains to map city roads as effectively as highways, it remains a vital step forward.

For officials requiring immediate, flawless global mapping or hyper-specialised privacy frameworks, open-source architectures offer airtight backups. Applications like Organic Maps operate 100% offline with zero trackers, no data collection, and no server-side profiling.

Similarly, OsmAnd allows for local route computation and completely self-contained navigation built on community-vetted OpenStreetMap data layers, entirely bypassing corporate or state surveillance architectures.
Enforcing the digital perimeter

Enforcing this shift requires more than just voluntary compliance; it demands strict, centralised technical execution by government IT and cybersecurity teams. To plug this leak entirely, government agencies must deploy comprehensive mobile device management (MDM) profiles across all state-issued smartphones to centrally blacklist and auto-uninstall Waze.

Furthermore, government network administrators must implement strict DNS filtering and firewall blocks on secure public-sector Wi-Fi networks, cutting off telemetry to Waze's backend API servers entirely. Combined with application control policies on secure endpoints, these measures transition the policy from a simple guideline into an ironclad digital perimeter.
When a leaked database can expose millions, and foreign laws can compel the surrender of live location feeds, the choice for Malaysia's leadership is clear.

Convenience cannot trump national sovereignty. Enforcing a strict digital perimeter – beginning with the immediate removal of Waze from every official device – is not a matter of lifestyle preference.
It represents a vital, immediate act of national security and digital defence.

0a7b828c3e2e299a: From S Murugesan
Last night, I used Waze to find a Japanese restaurant in Bukit Jalil. According to Putrajaya, I may have just put national security at risk.
Let me explain how we got here.
First, the government banned civil servants from using Waze. A circular from the Prime Minister's Department cited the app's links to Israel and data security concerns.

Like most Malaysians, I read the news with some amusement and went about my work. It didn't affect me. What the government wants its employees to do is its business, as long as it doesn't affect my life.

To be fair, I can accept the security argument. It's a known fact that data is mined from apps and social media platforms. Information about civil servants in key positions is sensitive, and I can understand the government being cautious.
Ban it for civil servants? Fine. Encourage Malaysians to use TuJu, our very own navigation app? Still fine. Nothing wrong with promoting local services.
Then the prime minister said the government may ban Waze completely for everyone.

A day later, digital minister Gobind Singh Deo said the ban applies only to civil servants on official duty. So which is it? If even the Cabinet cannot agree on how far this goes, ordinary Malaysians can be forgiven for being confused.
Let me be clear. Banning Waze for all of us would be overreach. The government shouldn't take away Malaysians' choices without a very good reason. So far, we haven't been given one.
Where is the evidence?

If the reason is security, kindly explain, in basic terms, how my using Waze to find a restaurant endangers the nation. I am already fully exposed on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, X and TikTok. What is one more app?
Waze, for its part, has publicly rejected the government's data security claims. If the government has evidence otherwise, please share it. Malaysians can handle the facts.
Why only Waze?
If Waze poses a special threat, tell us why it's being singled out. If the only issue is where the app was founded, then we're on a slippery slope.
Waze has been owned by Google since 2013. My data sits with the same company that runs Google Maps, YouTube and Gmail, and the Android system on most Malaysian phones.
Do we ban those next? Where does it stop?
Is TuJu any safer?
Here is the irony. If spyware like Pegasus, made by Israel's NSO Group, could break into iPhones, how long would it take a determined hacker to break into TuJu?
As an ordinary Malaysian, I would be more worried about my personal information in TuJu than in Waze.
If Waze can misuse my personal data, what is stopping TuJu from doing the same? Who runs TuJu? Who can see my data? Where is it stored?
These are fair questions. Answer them, and TuJu earns our trust. Ignore them, and no ban will fix that.
Let TuJu win on its own

If the real aim is to promote TuJu, the calculation is wrong. People resent being deprived of a choice, especially when they get little in return. Even Gobind told civil servants that if TuJu disappoints, they can use other apps, just not Waze. That is hardly a vote of confidence.

Look, I am happy that we now have our very own navigation app. I will try it. Just let me try it without restricting access to other apps. If, in due time, TuJu turns out to be more user-friendly and caters to my needs, I will use it, without the government pushing it down my throat. Take away my options, and I will resent it.
Competition will make TuJu better. A ban will only build resentment that might show in the next general election.
Build a better app, and Malaysians will find their way to it. No circular required.
S Murugesan is a lawyer and an FMT reader.

c636a8319993faee: Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.  “It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.  Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.  “Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.   Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.  “It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.  A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.  In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.  “As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”  That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking. “Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said. To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”  Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus. MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954. “He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”  She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”  Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”  Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University. Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).  In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.  Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”  For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.  “We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.  Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.  “I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.” She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

6643f32ed82d5f61: Using Google's products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world's largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won't use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company's privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.

On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. "We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos," the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.

Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads. Credit: Google This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it's shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it's also proving to be a privacy minefield.
60c7eb065c480fbc: At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society. The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.  “How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth. The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching. Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence. “AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.” In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024. “Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.” Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching. “MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science. Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone. “Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.” Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond  Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions. “We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee. The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students. Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching. “MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.” Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught. “I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said. During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans. “We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines.  “What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said. Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.”  “If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle. Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society. “I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.” Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future  The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production). “Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary. Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.” On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences. Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work. “SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said. Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health). “This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.” During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied.  “There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?” Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example. Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.” “A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said. As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event. “I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”
b2b7ebe6730fbedf: US chip champion Intel was so confused by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.” The tech company wanted to make sure that it could continue using certain robotic vehicles in its US chip fabs.

The uncertainty surrounding the Federal Communications Commission ban on certain foreign-made robots was revealed in the agency’s decision to grant Intel’s waiver request. On October 22, the FCC published its order allowing Intel to continue using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for a period of one year.

The robots in question are automated guided vehicles operating on “tracks or predefined paths” while often requiring operator oversight, according to Intel’s website. They help to move materials and items around within warehouses and factory floors.
99dfbeba275d12c7: Israeli police disperse ultra-Orthodox Jews blocking a road during a protest against the army draft in Jerusalem on Oct. 8, 2026. AP Photo/Ohad ZwigenbergOn Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called “unacceptable.” The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis. A 2024 court ruling that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate. Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying should enlist. With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters want Haredi communities to share the burden. Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future. Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system. Growing population Haredi Jews strictly observe Jewish religious law and often disapprove of liberal interpretations. They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – six children, on average – and about half of the men devote themselves to full-time religious study. The poverty rate is 33%, more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews. The Israeli public is about 14% Haredi, but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate. Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi by 2050. People walk the streets of the ultra-Orthodox neighborhood Mea Shearim in Jerusalem, Israel, on April 18, 2024. AP Photo/Leo Correa Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties. Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors came from northern and eastern Europe – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula and the Middle East, are linked to Shas. A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was formed in July 2026. The party says it will represent Haredim who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ, emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system. Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has included women on its candidate list. Conservative allies Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use a proportional representation system. Any party that receives more than 3.25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received. Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections. Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset. Shas and UTJ have agreed to share their surplus votes in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share. Orthodox Jews walk past an election campaign banner for the Haredi religious political party Shas, bearing a portrait of former Sephardi Chief Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, in Jerusalem on Oct. 15, 2026. John Wessels/ AFP via Getty Images Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats. No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself. As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team. Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most governing coalitions for the past two decades, with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. Haredi parties are seen as strong conservative allies, and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations. Today, as Netanyahu faces challenges from other right-wing parties over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more. Landmark ruling The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power. For many years, one of their priorities has been draft exemptions for religious education. Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although Muslim and Christian Arab citizens are generally exempted. Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a costly demonstration of commitment to the state. Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years. Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training. For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions. It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities. Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive government payments for each student. Given the communities’ low employment rates, large families and high poverty rates, many families rely on public support. In 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that a blanket exemption from military service for Haredim was not legal. Netanyahu’s government struggled to enact a compromise between those who favored drafting Haredim and the Haredi parties; the failure to find a lasting legal way to exempt Haredi men led Shas and UTJ to leave the Likud-led coalition in 2025. Ultra-Orthodox Jewish men protest military recruitment by blocking a road in Bnei Brak, near Tel Aviv, Israel, on July 16, 2024. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg Growing tensions Nonetheless, this ruling has not led to mass conscription. Haredi groups have held public protests, and many have ignored draft notices. While tens of thousands of men are draft eligible but not serving, and most of them are Haredi, fewer than 500 evaders have been arrested in 2026. Netanyahu argues against arrests, saying they discourage men from enlisting without coercion. In July 2026, at the urging of Haredi parties, the government passed a law to temporarily prevent arresting draft evaders. Some members of Netanyahu’s governing coalition opposed the law, however, and right-wing opposition parties filed petitions to challenge it in court. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – leader of the Together alliance, and seen as a key contender to oust Netanyahu – has threatened to cut subsidies to the Haredi community if they continue to defy the draft. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, is another top contender to replace Netanyahu. He has proposed allowing 3% of Haredi men exemptions to study, while drafting the majority. As the number of conflict zones increases – Gaza, southern Lebanon and Iran, as well as deployments in the West Bank – the unequal burden of military participation is a growing source of resentment among many conscripted Israelis and their families. Seven in 10 Jewish Israelis favor drafting the Haredim. Shas and UTJ, however, have declared they will not join a coalition unless it promises to codify the draft exemption into law. Shifting coalitions When the Haredi parties exited Netanyahu’s coalition, Likud replaced them with nationalist parties that emphasize the state and Jewish supremacy. Particularly notable was the decision to include the Jewish Power party, an offshoot of an earlier group banned for racism; including Kahanist groups was long seen as a red line. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, seen here with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023, is also head of the Jewish Power party. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg Haredi communities, on the other hand, tend to prioritize religious Jewishness over the state. Most Haredim do not consider themselves Zionist, and a small percentage are anti-Zionist. They argue that it was sacrilegious for people to create a state of Israel rather than waiting for God to return Jews to the land of Israel. Where nationalist politicians emphasize the secular state and military service, Haredim see their religious study as service to the Jewish community. As Likud’s changing coalition shows, Netanyahu’s alliances are strategic rather than ideological. I believe his decision to side with the Haredim on the recent draft legislation suggests his coalition is open to revision after the October 2026 election. As the Haredi community grows, its power in the electoral system will become less disproportionate. In a democratic framework, a large social group would deserve proportional representation and influence. As such, the tension between their electoral power, their demands for exemptions and subsidies, and the tolerance of non-Haredi Jews will persist as a political challenge.
